summary: Describes two LDAPv3 control extensions for server-side sorting of search results. A client names the attribute types and matching rules the server should use when returning results. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of getting a pile of search results and sorting them yourself, you ask the directory to hand them over already in order.

questions: what is ldap server side sorting
how does the ldap sort control work
what happens if an ldap server cannot sort results
subtitle: How an LDAP client asks the directory server to hand back search results already sorted, and how the server says whether it did.

tldr.problem: Some LDAP clients are too limited to sort search results themselves, or otherwise cannot, but still need the entries in a particular order.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a request control listing sort keys (attribute type, optional matching rule, optional reverse flag) to its search. The server answers with a response control carrying a sort result code.
tldr.outcome: The client can trust the order only if the response control says success. If the control is missing, the client should assume the sort was ignored.

today: RFC 2891 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Controls for Sorted Results
sections.content:
RFC 2891 defines two LDAPv3 controls: extra pieces of data attached to an LDAP message. Together they let a client say which attribute types and matching rules a server should use when it returns the results of a search. The RFC says this may be useful when the client has limited functionality or otherwise cannot sort the results but still needs them sorted.

The pair is a request control, sent with the search, and a response control, returned with the final search result. Because the response control has its own result code, the server can report how the sorting went independently of the result code for the search itself. Other controls that may appear on searches are not defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the librarian a note saying how to line the books up. The librarian sends back a note saying whether it worked.

sections.title: The Request Control
sections.content:
The request control rides in the controls field of the searchRequest message. Its controlType is 1.2.840.113556.1.4.473. The client may set criticality to TRUE or FALSE; an absent value counts as FALSE. The controlValue is the BER encoding of a SortKeyList, a sequence of keys.

Each key has an attributeType, an optional orderingRule (a matching rule id) and a reverseOrder flag that defaults to FALSE. The list runs from highest to lowest sort key precedence.

  • The matching rule SHOULD be valid for its attribute type, otherwise the server returns inappropriateMatching.
  • If the ordering rule is omitted, the ordering matching rule defined for the attribute MUST be used.
  • An attribute type should appear only once; if repeated, the server should return unwillingToPerform.
  • Any conformant implementation MUST accept a list with at least one key.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists what to sort by first, what to sort by if two are tied, and whether to go backwards. Each thing should be on the list only once.

sections.title: The Response Control
sections.content:
The server puts the response control in the searchResultDone message. Its controlType is 1.2.840.113556.1.4.474 and criticality is FALSE (it may be absent). The value is a BER-encoded SortResult: an enumerated sortResult code plus an optional attributeType.

The code success (0) means the results are sorted. The other codes explain failures, for example timeLimitExceeded (3), strongAuthRequired (8, refused to return sorted results over an insecure protocol), adminLimitExceeded (11, too many entries to sort), noSuchAttribute (16), inappropriateMatching (18), insufficientAccessRights (50), busy (51), unwillingToPerform (53) and other (80).

On an error, the server MAY set attributeType to the first attribute type in the list that was at fault. The client SHOULD ignore that field when the result is success.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply note has a number for how it went: 0 means sorted, other numbers say what went wrong, and it may point at the bad item on your list.

sections.title: The Six Scenarios
sections.content:
The server SHOULD return all results in the order given by the sort keys, reversed per key if reverseOrder is TRUE. The RFC lists six cases, depending on whether the server supports the control, whether it can sort with the given keys, and whether the client marked the control critical.

  • Unsupported, critical: the server MUST return unavailableCriticalExtension in searchResultDone and send no other results.
  • Unsupported, not critical: the server MUST ignore the control and process the search normally.
  • Supported but cannot sort, critical: the server SHOULD return unavailableCriticalExtension, include the response control, and send no entries.
  • Supported but cannot sort, not critical: the server returns all results unsorted and includes the response control.
  • Can sort: the server includes the response control with success.
  • Search failed or returned no entries: the server SHOULD omit the response control.

The client is assured of the order if and only if the result code is success. If the response control is absent, the client SHOULD assume the server ignored the sort control. Servers may also limit how many keys they accept, for example only one.
sections.plainLanguage: If the librarian cannot sort, you either get nothing (if you said it was a must) or an unsorted pile with a note saying so (if you did not). If there is no note at all, assume nobody sorted anything.

sections.title: Chaining, Missing Keys and Paged Results
sections.content:
If a server chains the request to other servers and the client made the control critical, the server MUST merge sort the combined results or MUST return unwillingToPerform.

An entry missing a sort key is treated as having a NULL value, and NULL is considered larger than every valid value. With one key, such entries come after all others, or before all others if reverseOrder is set. For a multi-valued attribute, the server SHOULD use the least value according to the attribute's ordering rule, when no other controls affect the order.

When combined with the paged results control from RFC 2696, the server should sort the entire result set, not each page separately. The sort key list must be present on every page request and must not change. The server SHOULD send the response control on every page so clients can tell quickly whether the set is sorted.
sections.plainLanguage: Things with no value to sort by go at the end of the line. If the answers come in pages, the whole pile is sorted first, not each page on its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sorting can let a client pull many records out of a directory despite administrative limits on how many records a search may return. A client wanting every record could combine sorting with updated search filters to fetch the whole database in small result sets.

The RFC says this can be countered by careful use of permissions on directory entries and by intelligent implementations of the administrative limits.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone may only take a few books at a time, sorting could help them sneak out the whole shelf a few at a time, so the librarian must watch for that.

items.label: timeLimitExceeded
items.desc: Time limit reached before sorting was completed.

items.label: strongAuthRequired
items.desc: Refused to return sorted results via an insecure protocol.

items.label: adminLimitExceeded
items.desc: Too many matching entries for the server to sort.

items.label: noSuchAttribute
items.desc: Unrecognized attribute type in sort key.

items.label: inappropriateMatching
items.desc: Unrecognized or inappropriate matching rule in sort key.

items.label: insufficientAccessRights
items.desc: Refused to return sorted results to this client.
